'''Ancient Macedonian''' was either an [[ancient Greek dialect]]<ref name="Christesen&Murray2010"/><ref name="Anson2010"/><ref>{{cite book|last=Obrador-Cursach|first=Bartomeu|title=The Phrygian Language|publisher=BRILL|year=2022|volume=139|series=Handbook of Oriental Studies. Section 1 The Near and Middle East|page=121|quote=The Thracian corpus is too short to give an overview of this language and Macedonian is better explained as a Greek dialect than a proper language (...).|isbn=9789004419995|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PghZEAAAQBAJ}}</ref>—part of [[Northwest Greek|Northwest]]<ref name="Giannakis2017-18"/><ref name="vanBeek2022" /><ref name="Crespo2023"/> or [[Aeolic Greek]]<ref name="Sowa2022"/>—or a [[Hellenic languages|Hellenic language]]<ref name="Joseph2001"/><ref name="Blazek2005"/> spoken by the [[ancient Macedonians]] during the 1st millennium BC. Spoken originally in the kingdom of [[Macedon]], it gradually fell out of use during the 4th century BC, marginalized by the [[Government of Macedonia (ancient kingdom)|Macedonian aristocracy]]'s use of [[Attic Greek]], the dialect that became the basis of [[Koine Greek]], the [[lingua franca]] of the [[Hellenistic period]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Borza |first=Eugene N. |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=614pd07OtfQC&pg=PA94 |title=In the Shadow of Olympus: The Emergence of Macedon |chapter=Who Were the Macedonians? |date=28 September 1992 |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]] |isbn=978-0-691-00880-6 |orig-date=1990 |publication-date=1992 |page=94 |language=en |quote=One can only speculate that that [Ancient Macedonian] dialect declined with the rise in use of standard ''koinē'' Greek. The main language of formal discourse and official communication became Greek by the fourth century [BC]. Whether the dialect(s) were eventually replaced by standard Greek, or were preserved as part of a two–tiered system of speech—one for official use, the other idiomatic for traditional ceremonies, rituals, or rough soldiers' talk—is problematic and requires more evidence and further study.}}</ref> It became [[Extinct language|extinct]] during either the Hellenistic or [[Roman imperial period (chronology)|Roman imperial]] period, and was entirely replaced by Koine Greek.<ref>{{harvnb|Engels|2010|p=94}}: "However, with respect to the discussion in this chapter it seems to be quite clear that (a) ancient Macedonian at some date during the Hellenistic or Roman imperial era was completely replaced by ''koine'' Greek and died out, and (b) that ancient Macedonian has no relationship with modern Macedonian which together with Bulgarian belongs to the eastern branch of southern Slavonic languages."</ref>

While the bulk of surviving public and private inscriptions found in ancient Macedonia were written in Attic Greek (and later in Koine Greek),<ref>{{harvnb|Engels|2010|p=94}}: "Many surviving public and private inscriptions indicate that in the Macedonian kingdom there was no dominant written language but standard Attic and later on ''koine'' Greek."</ref><ref name="CambridgeAncientHistory">{{cite book|title=The Cambridge ancient history, 3rd edition, Volume VI|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2000|page=730|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vx251bK988gC&pg=RA7-PA831 | first1=D. == Classification ==
Scholars have variously proposed that ancient Macedonian was a dialect of Greek, a sister language or an independent Indo-European language, and the disputes have sometimes had modern nationalistic overtones.<ref name="OxfordClassicalDictionary" /> Research has also considered the extent of influence from Thessalian Aeolic Greek and non-Greek substrata or adstrata, such as Phrygian, Illyrian, and Thracian. == Properties ==
Because of the fragmentary sources of Ancient Macedonian, only a little is understood about the special features of the language. The phonology of Greek}}</ref>). K. |title=Encyclopedia of Ancient Greek Language and Linguistics |pages=56–59 |edition=II |url=https://referenceworks.brillonline.com/entries/encyclopedia-of-ancient-greek-language-and-linguistics/*-COM_00000154#d19833870e372 |doi=10.1163/2214-448X_eagll_COM_00000154 |chapter=Greek and Illyrian|date=23 December 2013 }}</ref>{{sfn|Filos|2017|p=235}} Filos, however, notes, that the attribution of {{angbr|β}}, {{angbr|δ}} and {{angbr|γ}} for specifically voiced stops is not secure.{{sfn|Filos|2017|p=235}} Simon Hornblower writes: "Little is known about how Macedonian Greek was spoken, except that for instance 'Philip' was pronounced 'Bilip' (...)."<ref>{{cite book | last = Hornblower | first = Simon | chapter = Macedon, Thessaly and Boiotia | title = The Greek World, 479–323 BC | publisher = Routledge | date = 2011 | edition = Fourth | page = 96 | quote = Little is known about how Macedonian Greek was spoken, except that for instance 'Philip' was pronounced 'Bilip' (...).}}</ref>

If '''{{lang|xmk|γοτάν}}''' ''gotán'' ('pig') is related to the [[Proto-Hellenic]] noun {{wikt-lang|grk-x-proto|*gʷous}}, and hence to the [[Proto-Indo-European language|PIE]] noun {{wikt-lang|ine-x-proto|*gʷṓws}} ('cattle'), this would indicate that the [[labialized velar consonant|labiovelars]] were either intact, or merged with the velars, unlike the usual Greek treatment (Attic '''{{lang|grc-x-attic|βοῦς}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|boûs}}). Such deviations, however, are not unknown in Greek dialects; compare [[Doric Greek#Laconian|Laconian Doric]] (the dialect of Sparta) '''{{lang|grc-x-doric|γλεπ-}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|glep-}} for common Greek '''{{lang|grc-x-koine|βλεπ-}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|blep-}}, as well as Doric '''{{lang|grc-x-doric|γλάχων}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|gláchōn}} and [[Ionic Greek|Ionic]] '''{{lang|grc-x-ionic|γλήχων}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|glēchōn}} for common Greek '''{{lang|grc-x-koine|βλήχων}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|[[Mentha pulegium|blēchōn]]}}.<ref name="Stuttgart-1930">Albrecht von Blumenthal, ''Hesychstudien'', Stuttgart, 1930, 21.</ref>
A number of examples suggest that voiced [[Velar consonant|velar]] stops were devoiced, especially word-initially: '''{{lang|xmk|κάναδοι}}''' ''kánadoi'', 'jaws' (< PIE {{lang|ine-x-proto|*genu-}}); '''{{lang|xmk|κόμβους}}''' {{Transliteration|xmk|kómbous}}, 'molars' (< PIE {{lang|ine-x-proto|*gombh-}}); within words: '''{{lang|xmk|ἀρκόν}}''' ''arkón'' (Attic '''{{lang|grc-x-attic|ἀργός}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|argós}}); the Macedonian [[toponym]] {{Transliteration|xmk|Akesamenai}}, from the [[Pierian Mountains|Pierian]] name ''Akesamenos'' (if ''Akesa-'' is cognate to Greek {{Transliteration|grc|agassomai}}, {{Transliteration|grc|agamai}}, "to astonish"; cf. the Thracian name {{Transliteration|txh|Agassamenos}}).
In [[Aristophanes]]' [[The Birds (play)|''The Birds'']], the form '''{{lang|grc|κεβλήπυρις}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|keblēpyris}} ('red head', the name of a bird, perhaps the [[European goldfinch|goldfinch]] or [[redpoll]]) is found,<ref>[https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/cgi-bin/ptext?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0058%3Aentry%3D%2317647 Henry George Liddell, Robert Scott, An Intermediate Greek-English Lexicon, κεβλήπυρις]. Perseus.tufts.edu. Retrieved on 2013-07-21.</ref> showing a Macedonian-style voiced stop in place of a standard Greek unvoiced aspirate: '''{{lang|xmk|κεβ(α)λή}}''' {{Transliteration|xmk|keb(a)lē}} versus '''{{lang|grc|κεφαλή}}''' {{Transliteration|grc|kephalē}} ('head').

A number of the Macedonian words, particularly in [[Hesychius of Alexandria]]'s lexicon, are disputed (i.e., some do not consider them actual Macedonian words) and some may have been corrupted in the transmission. Thus ''abroutes'' may be read as {{Transliteration|xmk|abrouwes}} ({{lang|xmk|αβρουϝες}}), with tau ({{lang|xmk|Τ}}) replacing a [[digamma]].<ref>Olivier Masson, "Sur la notation occasionnelle du digamma grec par d'autres consonnes et la glose macédonienne abroutes", ''Bulletin de la Société de linguistique de Paris'', 90 (1995) 231–239. Also proposed by O. Hoffmann and J. Kalleris.</ref> If so, this word would perhaps be encompassable within a Greek dialect; however, others (e.g. [[Antoine Meillet|A. Meillet]]) see the dental as authentic and think that this specific word would perhaps belong to an Indo-European language different from Greek.{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}

Emilio Crespo, a researcher at the [[Autonomous University of Madrid]], concludes that: "the inscriptions from [[Aegae (Macedonia)|Aigeai]], the ancient capital of the Macedonian kingdom, and from the other regions ([[Pieria (regional unit)#History|Pieria]], [[Beroea|Beroia]] and [[Eordaea|Eordaia]]) that formed the core of the ancient [[Argead dynasty|Temenid]] kingdom show occasional instances{{nbsp}}... in which {{angbr|β δ γ}} appear instead of  {{angbr|ɸ θ χ}} or  of {{angbr|π τ κ}}, respectively", while "similar examples are also attested in northern [[Ancient Thessaly|Thessaly]]".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Crespo |first=Emilio |chapter=Dialects in Contact in the Ancient Kingdom of Macedon |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bczbEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA73 |title=Alloglōssoi: Multilingualism and Minority Languages in Ancient Europe |date=2023 |publisher=[[De Gruyter]] |isbn=978-3-11-077968-4 |editor-last=Cassio |editor-first=Albio Cesare |language=en |editor-last2=Kaczko |editor-first2=Sara |page=77|quote=The inscriptions from Aigeai, the ancient capital of the Macedonian kingdom, and from the other regions (Pieria, Beroia and Eordaia) that formed the core of the ancient Temenid kingdom show occasional instances from the 4th cent. BCE in which the graphemes {{angbr|Β, Δ, Γ}} appear instead of {{angbr|Φ, Θ, Χ}} or of {{angbr|Π, Τ, Κ}}, respectively. Similar examples are also attested in northern Thessaly}}</ref> Emilio Crespo wrote that "the voicing of voiceless stops and the development of aspirates into voiced fricatives turns out to be the outcome of an internal development of Macedonian as a dialect of Greek", without excluding "the presence of interference from other languages or of any linguistic substrate or adstrate", as also argued by M. Hatzopoulos.{{sfn|Crespo|2017|p=344}}

Hatzopoulos supports the hypothesis of a (North-)'[[Mycenaean Greece|Achaean]]' substratum extending as far north as the head of the [[Thermaic Gulf]], which had a continuous relation, in prehistoric times, both in [[Ancient Thessaly|Thessaly]] and [[Macedonia (ancient kingdom)|Macedonia]], with the Northwest Greek-speaking populations living on the other side of the [[Pindus]] mountain range, and contacts became cohabitation when the Argead Macedonians completed their wandering from [[Orestis (region)|Orestis]] to Lower Macedonia in the 7th c. BC. According to this hypothesis, Hatzopoulos concludes that the Ancient Macedonian dialect of the historical period, attested in inscriptions such as Pella curse tablet, is a sort of koine resulting from the interaction and the influences of various elements, the most important of which are the North-Achaean substratum, the [[Northwest Greek]] dialect of the [[Argead Macedonians]], and the [[Thracian language|Thracian]] and [[Phrygian language|Phrygian]] adstrata.{{sfn|Hatzopoulos|2017|pp=321–322}} [[Claude Brixhe]]  espoused the hypothesis "of a sporadic secondary voicing of unvoiced consonants within the history of [[Greek language|Greek]]", in agreement with Hatzopoulos.<ref>{{cite book |last=Brixhe |first=Claude |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SuR8DwAAQBAJ |title=Handbook of Comparative and Historical Indo-European Linguistics |date=2018 |publisher=[[De Gruyter]] |isbn=978-3-11-054243-1 |editor1-last=Klein |editor1-first=Jared |volume=3 |pages=1864–1865 |language=en |chapter=Macedonian |author-link=Claude Brixhe |editor2-last=Joseph |editor2-first=Brian |editor3-last=Fritz |editor3-first=Matthias|quote=Far more worthy of consideration is the view adopted by Hatzopoulos (most recently 2006: 41–46), who supposes a Greek development *bh > ph > f > v.}}</ref><ref name="Hatzopoulos2020">{{harvnb|Hatzopoulos|2020|p=77}}: "Brixhe in two gallant and generous articles finally discarded the Phrygian hypothesis and espoused that of a sporadic secondary voicing of unvoiced consonants within the history of Greek, as I had contended for three decades. His present views, to most of which I gladly adhere, are the following: the conquering Argead Macedonians, who spoke a North-Western Greek dialect, upon their descent from Mount Pindos down to the plains, met Achaean Greeks intermingled with non-Greek speakers. The substitution of the letter sign of the voiced stop for that of the voiceless 'aspirate' cannot be explained by the hypothetical survival of the Indo-European voiced 'aspirate' stops of their non-'aspirate' reflex."</ref>

A. Panayotou summarizes some features generally identified through ancient texts and epigraphy:<ref name="Greek 2007 pp. 439-441">A history of ancient Greek: from the beginnings to late antiquity, Maria Chritē, Maria Arapopoulou, Cambridge University Press (2007), pp. 439–441</ref>

===Phonology===
*Occasional development of voiced aspirates (*bʰ, *dʰ, *gʰ) into voiced stops (b, d, g) (e.g. Βερενίκα, Attic Φερενίκη)
*Retention of <nowiki>*</nowiki>/aː/ (e.g. Μαχάτας), also present in [[Doric Greek#Epirotic|Epirotic]]<ref name="epigraphy.packhum.org">[http://epigraphy.packhum.org/inscriptions//main Packard Institute epigraphic database] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071121221117/http://epigraphy.packhum.org/inscriptions/main |date=2007-11-21 }}</ref>
*[aː] as a result of contraction between [aː] and [ɔː]
*Apocope of short vowels in prepositions in synthesis ({{lang|xmk|παρκαττίθεμαι}}, Attic {{lang|grc-x-attic|παρακατατίθεμαι}})
*Syncope (hyphairesis) and diphthongization are used to avoid hiatus (e.g. {{lang|xmk|Θετίμα}}, Attic {{lang|grc-x-attic|Θεοτίμη}}; compare with Epirotic {{lang|grc|Λαγέτα}}, Doric {{lang|grc-x-doric|Λαογἐτα}}).<ref name="epigraphy.packhum.org" />
*Occasional retention of the pronunciation [u] of /u(ː)/ in local cult epithets or nicknames ({{lang|xmk|Κουναγίδας}} = {{lang|xmk|Κυναγίδας}})
*Raising of /ɔː/ to /uː/ in proximity to nasal (e.g. {{lang|xmk|Κάνουν}}, Attic {{lang|grc-x-attic|Κανών}})
*Simplification of the sequence /ign/ to /iːn/ (γίνομαι, Attic {{lang|grc-x-attic|γίγνομαι}})
*Loss of aspiration of the consonant cluster /stʰ/ (> /st/) ({{lang|xmk|γενέσται}}, Attic {{lang|grc-x-attic|γενέσθαι}})

=== Morphology ===
Ancient Macedonian morphology is shared with [[Epirus (ancient state)|ancient Epirus]], including some of the oldest inscriptions from [[Dodona]].<ref>Eric Lhote (2006) Les lamelles Oraculaires de Dodone. Droz, Geneve.</ref> The morphology of the first declension nouns with an -ας ending is also shared with [[Thessalian Greek|Thessalian]] (e.g. Epitaph for Pyrrhiadas, Kierion<ref>Roberts, E.S., An Introduction to Greek Epigraphy vol. 1 no. 237</ref>).
*First-declension masculine and feminine in -ας and -α respectively (e.g. {{lang|xmk|Πευκέστας}}, {{lang|xmk|Λαομάγα}})
*First-declension masculine genitive singular in -α (e.g. {{lang|xmk|Μαχάτα}})
*First-declension genitive plural in -ᾶν
*First person personal pronoun dative singular {{lang|xmk|ἐμίν}}
*Temporal conjunction {{lang|xmk|ὁπόκα}}
*Possibly, a non-sigmatic nominative masculine singular in the first declension ({{lang|xmk|ἱππότα}}, Attic {{lang|grc-x-attic|ἱππότης}})

=== Onomastics ===

==== Anthroponymy ====
M. Hatzopoulos and Johannes Engels summarize the Macedonian anthroponymy (that is names borne by people from Macedonia before the expansion beyond the [[Vardar|Axios]] or people undoubtedly hailing from this area after the expansion) as follows:<ref>Greek Personal Names: Their Value as Evidence, [[Elaine Matthews]], Simon Hornblower, Peter Marshall Fraser, British Academy, Oxford University Press (2000), p. 103</ref>{{sfn|Engels|2010|pp=94–95}}

*Epichoric (local) Greek names that either differ from the phonology of the introduced Attic or that remained almost confined to Macedonians throughout antiquity
*Panhellenic (common) Greek names
*Identifiable non-Greek (Thracian and Illyrian) names
*Names without a ''clear'' Greek etymology that can't however be ascribed to any identifiable non-Greek linguistic group.

Common in the creation of ethnics is the use of -έστης, -εστός especially when derived from sigmatic nouns ({{lang|xmk|ὄρος > Ὀρέστης}} but also {{lang|xmk|Δῖον > Διασταί}}).<ref name="Greek 2007 pp. 439-441" />

Per Engels, the above material supports that Macedonian anthroponymy was predominantly Greek in character.{{sfn|Engels|2010|pp=94–95}}

==== Toponymy ====
The toponyms of Macedonia proper are generally Greek, though some of them show a particular phonology and a few others are non-Greek.

=== Calendar ===
{{Further|Ancient Macedonian calendar}}
The Macedonian calendar's origins go back to [[History of Greece|Greek prehistory]]. The names of the Macedonian months, just like most of the names of Greek months, are derived from feasts and related celebrations in honor of the [[Greek gods]]. Most of them combine a Macedonian dialectal form with a clear Greek etymology (e.g {{lang|xmk|Δῐός}} from [[Zeus]]; {{lang|xmk|Περίτιος}} from [[Heracles]] Peritas ("Guardian"); {{lang|xmk|Ξανδικός/Ξανθικός}} from Xanthos, "the blond" (probably a reference to Heracles); {{lang|xmk|Άρτεμίσιος}} from [[Artemis]] etc.) with the possible exception of one, which is attested in other [[Ancient Greek calendars|Greek calendars]] as well. According to [[Martin P. Nilsson]], the Macedonian calendar is formed like a regular Greek one and the names of the months attest the Greek nationality of the Macedonians.{{sfn|Hatzopoulos|2020|p=78}}

About 99% of the roughly 6,300 inscriptions discovered by archaeologists within the confines of ancient Macedonia were written in the Greek language, using the [[Greek alphabet]]. The legends in all currently discovered coins are also in Greek.<ref name="Anson2010"/> The [[Pella curse tablet]], a text written in a distinct [[Doric Greek]] dialect, found in 1986 and dated to between mid to early 4th century BC, has been forwarded as an argument that ancient Macedonian was a dialect of North-Western Greek, part of the Doric dialect group.<ref name="Engels2010-95" /><ref>"...{{nbsp}}but we may tentatively conclude that Macedonian is a dialect related to North-West Greek.", Olivier Masson, French linguist, "Oxford Classical Dictionary: Macedonian Language", 1996.</ref>

=== Hesychius' glossary ===

The majority of these words can be confidently assigned to Greek albeit some words would appear to reflect a dialectal form of Greek. === Macedonian in Classical sources ===
{{further information|Greek historiography}}
In his comedy ''The Macedonians'', the 5th century BC Athenian poet [[Strattis]] has a character speak in a non-[[Attic]] dialect, but little has survived.{{sfn|Hatzopoulos|2017|p=309}}

In his history ''[[Ab Urbe Condita (book)|Ab urbe condita]]'' [[Livy]] (59 BC – 14 AD) has a Macedonian ambassador in the late 3rd century BC argue that Aetolians, [[Acarnania]]ns and Macedonians were "men of the same language".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Titus Livius (Livy), The History of Rome, Book 31, chapter 29 |url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Liv.+31+29&fromdoc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0148 |access-date=5 January 2025 |website=www.perseus.tufts.edu |at=paragraph 15}}</ref>

In his ''[[Histories of Alexander the Great]]'', [[Quintus Curtius Rufus]] (1st century AD) relates an argument between Alexander and Philotas, an accused man, as to whether Philotas should address those assembled in a "foreign tongue" ({{lang|la|peregrina lingua}}) or his "native idiom" ({{lang|la|patrius sermo}}).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Curtius Rufus |first1=Quintus |title=The history of Alexander |last2=Curtius Rufus |first2=Quintus |date=2004 |publisher=Penguin Books |isbn=978-0-14-044412-4 |editor-last=Yardley |editor-first=John |edition=Repr. with updated bibliography |series=Penguin classics |location=London |at=6.9.34–6.9.36, 6.10.23}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Engels|2010|p=95}}: "Philotas is mocked in the Assembly of Macedonians for not speaking in Macedonian."</ref>

In his ''[[Arrian#Ta met' Alexandron|History of the Diadochi]]'', Arrian ({{floruit|1st century AD}}) says that in 321 BC the Greek general Eumenes sent a man who spoke Macedonian to convince the opposing Macedonian troops that their position was hopeless.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bosworth |first1=A. Brian |date=1978 |title=Eumenes, Neoptolemus and PSI XII 1284 |journal=GRBS |volume=19 |pages=227–237}}</ref><ref name="Kapetanopoulos1993">{{Cite journal |last=Kapetanopoulos |first=Elias |orig-date=1993 |publication-date=1995 |title=Xennias, μακεδονίζων τῇ φωνῇ |url=https://www.archetai.gr/images/pdfs/efimeris/Publ_A.E._1993.pdf |journal=Archaiologike Ephemeris |language=en, grc |publisher=[[Archaeological Society of Athens]] |volume=132 |pages=13–30}}</ref>

In his ''Life of Antony'',<ref name="perseus.tufts.edu">{{Cite web |title=Plutarch, Antony, chapter 27, section 4 |url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:2008.01.0077:chapter=27:section=4 |access-date=31 October 2025 |website=www.perseus.tufts.edu}}</ref> [[Plutarch]] (c. AD 40 – 120s) presents [[Cleopatra]] (70/69 – 30 BC) as speaking many foreign languages, in contrast with her royal predecessors, some of whom had even ceased to "Macedonise" ({{lang|grc|μακεδονίζειν}}, {{transliteration|grc|makedonizein}}).<ref name="perseus.tufts.edu"/>

== Influence==
{{further information|Koine Greek|Ancient Macedonians}}
As a consequence of the Macedonians' role in the formation of the Koine, Macedonian contributed considerable elements, unsurprisingly including some military terminology ({{lang|grc|διμοιρίτης, ταξίαρχος, ὑπασπισταί}}, etc.). Among the many contributions were the general use of the first declension grammar for male and female nouns with an -as ending, attested in the genitive of Macedonian coinage from the early 4th century BC of [[Amyntas III of Macedon|Amyntas III]] ({{lang|xmk|ΑΜΥΝΤΑ}} in the genitive; the Attic form that fell into disuse would be {{lang|grc|ΑΜΥΝΤΟΥ}}). There were changes in verb conjugation such as in the Imperative {{lang|xmk|δέξα}} attested in Macedonian sling stones found in Asiatic battlefields, that became adopted in place of the Attic forms. Koine Greek established a spirantisation of beta, gamma and delta, which has been attributed to the Macedonian influence.<ref>George Babiniotis (1992) The question of mediae in ancient Macedonian Greek reconsidered. In: Historical Philology: Greek, Latin, and Romance, Bela Brogyanyi, Reiner Lipp, 1992 John Benjamins Publishing)</ref> The term "Macedonian" ended up meaning the [[Koine Greek]] in classical sources.<ref>C. Brixhe, A. Panayotou, 1994, "Le Macédonien" in ''Langues indo-européennes'', p. 208.</ref>
